## What is checked

| Component           | Down when                                                 | Means                                                   |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Frontend**        | page doesn't load, or `id="root"` missing                 | server / gateway / DNS / SSL down, frontend not served  |
| **Shared Service**  | `/abc/core/api/v1/health` gives no JSON (502/504/timeout) | Shared backend process down                             |
| **Shared Database** | health body lacks `"database":"up"` (503)                 | Shared's Postgres unreachable — service itself still up |
| **AFS Service**     | `/abc/afs/api/v1/health` gives no JSON                    | AFS backend process down                                |
| **AFS Database**    | health body lacks `"database":"up"`                       | AFS's Postgres unreachable                              |
| **Cache (Redis)**   | _degraded_ (amber) when `"redis":"up"` is missing         | Redis down — the app keeps working, only slower         |

How to read it:

| What you see                                    | What broke                                            |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| Only **Shared Database** / **AFS Database** red | the database; services are up                         |
| **Shared Service** red (its Database red too)   | the Shared backend — DB state unknown while it's down |
| Everything red, Frontend too                    | the server / gateway / network                        |
| Only **Cache (Redis)** amber                    | Redis; users unaffected apart from speed              |

Health URLs live in repository secrets (`ABC_FRONTEND_URL`, `ABC_CORE_HEALTH_URL`, `ABC_AFS_HEALTH_URL`), so only component names are public.

**Not covered:** a single API returning 500 while `/health` is fine (Sentry catches that), a frontend JavaScript crash on a page that still loads, and outages shorter than the 5-minute check interval.

## Alerts and incidents

Alerts are **e-mail only**, to `insights-support@abcconsultants.in` (SMTP, configured through the `NOTIFICATION_EMAIL_SMTP*` repository secrets) — one mail when a component goes down or degraded, one when it recovers.

Upptime also keeps each incident as a locked GitHub issue; that is what the status page's incident history is built from. Nobody needs to watch or act on the issues.

## Posting incident updates

Updates shown under an incident on the status page are **comments on its GitHub issue**. Start each comment with its stage, then the message:

```
Investigating - We are looking into errors when exporting PBCs.
Identified - A timeout on large exports. Working on a fix.
Monitoring - A fix has been deployed and we are watching the exports.
Resolved - Exports are working normally again.
```

`Investigating`, `Identified`, `Monitoring`, `Update` and `Resolved` are recognised (bold or a colon is fine too: `**Monitoring:** …`); any other comment shows as an **Update**. Newest first, with its time in UTC. Markdown is shown as plain text.

- **Only the repository's owner, members and collaborators** (and the Upptime bot) appear on the page — a comment from anyone else is ignored.
- **An incident monitoring did not catch** (e.g. one screen failing while `/health` is fine): open an issue with the `status` label; its description is the first update. Add a component's label (`frontend`, `afs-service`, …) to also mark that component's day bar. Close the issue when it is over.

The page itself is `assets/status-ui.js` + `assets/status-ui.css` (wired in `.upptimerc.yml`); Upptime's incident pages are unchanged. The repository must be **public** — visitors' browsers read the status data and issues from GitHub directly.

## Docker (self-hosting the page)

Built like the ABC frontend's image: `node:20-alpine` + `serve@14.2.4` on port **4173** (`docker/Dockerfile`, routing in `docker/serve-config.sh`).

**Docker Image CI** (`.github/workflows/docker-image.yml`) runs after Upptime rebuilds the site on `gh-pages` (and on demand from the Actions tab), smoke-tests the image and pushes it to Docker Hub:

- `<DOCKER_USER>/abc-status:<gh-pages short sha>`
- `<DOCKER_USER>/abc-status:latest`

It needs the repository secrets **`DOCKER_USER`** and **`DOCKER_PASSWORDS`** (same names as in the frontend repo). The status data is read live from GitHub, so the image only changes when the site itself does.

The page lives at **https://insights.abcconsultants.in/status** — the app's own domain, under `/status`. On that server:

```sh
docker pull <DOCKER_USER>/abc-status:latest
docker rm -f abc-status 2>/dev/null
docker run -d --name abc-status --restart unless-stopped -p 127.0.0.1:4174:4173 <DOCKER_USER>/abc-status:latest
```

and in the nginx `server` block of `insights.abcconsultants.in`, **above** the frontend's `location /`:

```nginx
# Status page (abc-status container). The container serves the site under /status,
# so the path is passed through unchanged (no URI on proxy_pass).
location = /status { return 301 /status/; }
location /status/ {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:4174;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
}
```

**Base path.** `.upptimerc.yml` sets `cname: insights.abcconsultants.in` and `baseUrl: /status`, so Upptime builds the site for that address (stylesheet, links, error pages) and the image serves it under `/status`. Upptime also writes a CNAME file to `gh-pages`; GitHub Pages is no longer where the page lives, so unpublish it (Settings → Pages) once the server serves `/status`. A different path means changing `baseUrl`, the `scripts`/`links` URLs, and the repository variable `STATUS_BASE_PATH`.

Local build: `git archive origin/gh-pages | tar -x -C site` (in an empty `site/` at the repo root), then `docker build . -f docker/Dockerfile -t abc-status:local` and open http://127.0.0.1:4174/status/ after `docker run -p 4174:4173 abc-status:local`.
